messages.content: I want mobile manipulators to distinguish object slip from localization drift while they maintain contact during furniture repositioning. How should I state the goal without losing the two separate performance requirements?

The goal is to enable mobile manipulators to reposition furniture while maintaining contact and to tell whether an apparent discrepancy reflects object slip or localization drift. It has two distinct performance requirements: reposition unseen furniture within 5 cm in 90% of trials with intermittent visual occlusion, and identify slip versus localization drift with 90% balanced accuracy without external tracking during execution. The first requirement concerns repositioning performance; the second concerns distinguishing the two explanations.
What distinction matters between object slip and localization drift here?

They describe different kinds of discrepancy. Object slip concerns movement of the object relative to the contact involved in repositioning it. Localization drift concerns error in the manipulator’s estimate of where it is. The goal is not merely to notice that something seems inconsistent; it is to distinguish which of those two explanations applies while contact is maintained during furniture repositioning.
Does the goal say exactly how the manipulator should make that distinction?

No. It specifies the distinction the mobile manipulator must make and the required identification performance, but it does not prescribe a sensor, algorithm, decision rule, or control architecture. Those details would be additions rather than restatements of the goal.
I also want the contact condition to remain prominent. Is it just background context?

No. Maintaining contact is part of the goal: the manipulator is to distinguish object slip from localization drift while maintaining contact during furniture repositioning. It should not be paraphrased as a requirement to stop repositioning or release contact before making the distinction. The wording does not, however, give a separate numerical contact-maintenance threshold.
Can you unpack the repositioning target carefully?

The stated target is to reposition unseen furniture within 5 cm in 90% of trials, under intermittent visual occlusion. The 5 cm is the repositioning tolerance, and 90% of trials is the required frequency of meeting it. Intermittent visual occlusion is part of the condition under which that performance is sought; the target is not limited to trials with uninterrupted visibility.
Does 90% of trials mean that the manipulator must be within 5 cm for 90% of the time in each trial?

No. Those are different claims. The requirement is phrased as meeting the within-5-cm repositioning target in 90% of trials. It does not specify a percentage of time within each trial, or define a time-based tolerance.
What should we infer from the word ‘unseen’?

It is important to retain ‘unseen furniture’ in the requirement rather than quietly changing it to familiar furniture. The wording also specifies intermittent visual occlusion. It does not further define ‘unseen’—for example, it does not say precisely what prior exposure, if any, is excluded—so a restatement should avoid imposing a more specific interpretation.
And intermittent visual occlusion is not the same as a total absence of visual information, right?

Right. ‘Intermittent’ indicates that visual occlusion occurs at intervals; it does not state that vision is unavailable throughout execution. Equally, the repositioning requirement should not be simplified into one that assumes continuous visibility. The stated condition is intermittent visual occlusion, no more and no less.
Now explain the second number. What does 90% balanced accuracy say that plain accuracy would not?

Balanced accuracy gives the two categories equal weight when assessing identification performance. For a two-category slip-versus-localization-drift distinction, it is the average of the rate of correctly identifying slip and the rate of correctly identifying localization drift. That is why ‘90% balanced accuracy’ should be preserved rather than shortened to ‘90% accuracy’: the two phrases need not describe the same performance when the categories occur at different frequencies.
Could a system meet that target by calling every discrepancy slip?

Not if it is being evaluated on both slip and localization drift under the usual two-class definition of balanced accuracy. Always choosing slip would fail to identify localization drift, and balanced accuracy accounts for the recognition rate of each category. That explains the metric; it does not supply any observed result or say how the identification is implemented.
Does the 90% balanced-accuracy target also mean 90% of furniture-repositioning trials must individually have a correct slip-or-drift decision?

That would add a linkage the wording does not specify. The node gives a repositioning target of within 5 cm in 90% of trials and an identification target of 90% balanced accuracy. They are separate requirements. It does not state a joint success rate, a required number of decisions per trial, or that every repositioning success must also include a correct identification.
How restrictive is ‘without external tracking during execution’?

It means the slip-versus-localization-drift identification target must be met without relying on external tracking while the task is being executed. It does not name the resources that may be used instead, nor does it prescribe a particular way to assess performance. The important qualifier to preserve is ‘during execution’: the statement is specifically about reliance on external tracking at that time.
Should I say that external tracking is prohibited for every purpose, including any later evaluation?

No. That goes beyond the stated restriction. The requirement says ‘without external tracking during execution.’ It does not specify an evaluation procedure or make a broader claim about every possible use of external tracking outside execution.
Is the point to detect any error, or to say which of these two errors it is?

The point is to distinguish object slip from localization drift. A statement that the manipulator merely detects an anomaly would omit the requested identification. Conversely, the goal does not specify a more detailed list of error types beyond this distinction.
Can the two targets be merged into a sentence without making them sound like one metric?

Yes: ‘Enable mobile manipulators to maintain contact during furniture repositioning while distinguishing object slip from localization drift, with a target of repositioning unseen furniture within 5 cm in 90% of trials under intermittent visual occlusion and identifying slip versus localization drift with 90% balanced accuracy without external tracking during execution.’ That keeps both numerical targets and their respective conditions visible.
Would it be accurate to say those results have already been demonstrated?

No. The wording states a goal and requirements, not completed experiments or achieved results. ‘Target’ or ‘requirement’ is appropriate; ‘demonstrated’ would claim evidence that has not been supplied.
What are the easiest details to accidentally drop when I shorten it?

The main risks are dropping ‘unseen’ from the furniture requirement, omitting intermittent visual occlusion, turning ‘within 5 cm in 90% of trials’ into an imprecise accuracy claim, replacing 90% balanced accuracy with ordinary accuracy, or omitting ‘without external tracking during execution.’ A short version also needs to retain both maintaining contact and the distinction between object slip and localization drift.
What approach could connect the slip-versus-drift distinction to furniture control while the mobile manipulator maintains contact?

A proposed approach is to fuse tactile shear, wheel odometry, and intermittent RGB-D in a contact-constrained estimator. The estimator would distinguish object slip from localization drift, and that distinction would be used for furniture control. This is a proposal for how to approach the goal, not a claim that the estimator has been built or has achieved a particular result.
Why bring those three sources together rather than treating one as the answer?

They offer different kinds of information. Tactile shear concerns what is happening at contact; wheel odometry concerns the mobile base’s estimated motion; and RGB-D can provide visual and depth information when it is available. Fusing them is meant to let the estimator interpret a discrepancy across those perspectives rather than assuming that any single measurement, by itself, establishes whether the object slipped or localization drift occurred.
Could you explain ‘tactile shear’ here without assuming it proves slip?

Tactile shear refers to tangential information at the contact. That makes it relevant to a possible slip interpretation, but the proposal does not say that a particular shear reading is conclusive evidence of slip. Its role is as one input to an estimator that distinguishes slip from drift using the available information together.
What does wheel odometry add to that interpretation?

Wheel odometry supplies an estimate related to the mobile base’s motion. That gives the estimator a way to consider the manipulator’s estimated movement when interpreting what happens at contact and in the intermittent RGB-D observations. Odometry is an input to the distinction, not an independent guarantee that localization is correct or that a discrepancy must be object slip.
And is intermittent RGB-D supposed to be available the whole time?

No. ‘Intermittent RGB-D’ explicitly allows for times when those visual and depth observations are unavailable. The proposed fusion should be understood in that setting, rather than as a method that presumes a continuous RGB-D view. The proposal does not specify the timing of the available observations or a particular way of handling the gaps.
Does ‘contact-constrained’ mean the estimator assumes the furniture never slips?

It should not be read that way. Slip is one of the very conditions the estimator is proposed to distinguish from localization drift. ‘Contact-constrained’ indicates that maintaining contact matters to how the estimates are interpreted; it does not, by itself, specify a rigid no-slip assumption or rule slip out.
So contact is part of the estimation context as well as the control context?

Yes, at the level stated in the proposal. The estimator is contact-constrained, and its slip-versus-drift distinction is intended for furniture control during contact. The wording does not specify a particular mathematical contact constraint or a particular control action after either classification.
Would it be fair to describe the estimator as comparing what contact suggests with what motion and vision suggest?

That is a useful conceptual description, provided ‘comparing’ does not imply a specified calculation. Tactile shear, wheel odometry, and intermittent RGB-D can inform different aspects of the situation, and the proposed estimator fuses them to distinguish slip from drift. No exact comparison rule or decision threshold is given.
What is the difference between saying it distinguishes slip from drift and saying it corrects both?

Distinguishing them is the stated function of the estimator. ‘Corrects both’ would add a claimed capability: the proposal does not say how localization would be corrected, how slip would be remedied, or what furniture-control response would follow. It links the distinction to furniture control without specifying those further mechanisms.
Does the proposal establish that the three inputs always make the two explanations distinguishable?

No. It proposes fusing those inputs in a contact-constrained estimator for that purpose. It does not claim that every possible discrepancy can be resolved, particularly when some observations are intermittent, and it does not report measured identification performance.
I want to avoid making intermittent RGB-D sound like an external tracking system during execution. What can we actually say?

We can say only that intermittent RGB-D is one of the proposed inputs. The proposal does not specify the camera’s mounting, an external tracking arrangement, or an evaluation setup. The goal’s separate condition is to identify slip versus localization drift without external tracking during execution; the proposal should not be expanded into an unsupported claim about the exact hardware or evaluation procedure.
Can I call this a finished solution to the 5 cm and 90% targets?

No. The fusion approach is proposed for furniture control and the slip-versus-drift distinction. It contains no trial results and does not assert that unseen furniture has been repositioned within 5 cm in 90% of trials with intermittent visual occlusion, or that slip versus localization drift has been identified with 90% balanced accuracy without external tracking during execution.
Does ‘for furniture control’ imply that the estimator itself physically moves the furniture?

Not necessarily. The phrase says what the proposed distinction is intended to serve: furniture control. It does not define the division of responsibilities between estimation and control, or specify commands the manipulator would issue. Keeping ‘for furniture control’ conveys the intended use without inventing that interface.
How would you put the proposal in one sentence that stays within what is actually stated?

‘Fuse tactile shear, wheel odometry, and intermittent RGB-D in a contact-constrained estimator that distinguishes object slip from localization drift for furniture control.’ That states the three inputs, the estimator’s contact constraint, the distinction it is intended to make, and its intended use, without claiming a particular implementation or result.
If I said it uses RGB-D to determine the true furniture position and wheel odometry only to detect drift, would that be too specific?

Yes. The proposal names the inputs and the distinction they are to support, but it does not assign each input an exclusive function or designate RGB-D as ground truth. In particular, intermittent RGB-D should remain an input to the fused estimate, not be silently recast as an always-available definitive position measurement.
What is the central idea, then, when I explain it without adding a sensor design or a control policy?

The central idea is to interpret contact-related, base-motion, and intermittent visual-depth information together, under a contact-constrained estimation framing, so the mobile manipulator can distinguish object slip from localization drift in support of furniture control. That explanation captures the proposal while leaving the estimator design, control policy, and measured outcomes unspecified.
Which tactile–odometric residuals could distinguish gripper–furniture slip from map-frame localization drift during five-second RGB-D occlusions?

That is the open question. One candidate is a contact-consistency residual: compare what tactile shear suggests is happening at the gripper–furniture contact with what the estimated motion from wheel odometry would lead one to expect if contact were maintained without relative slip. A mismatch could be relevant to gripper–furniture slip. But the question does not specify a residual formula or establish that such a mismatch uniquely identifies slip. In particular, a drift of the map-frame pose estimate may not be visible in measurements that only describe relative motion at the contact.
What do you mean by a tactile–odometric residual, rather than just a tactile reading?

Conceptually, a residual is a difference between an observation and a prediction. Here, the prediction would use wheel-odometric motion together with an assumed contact relationship, while the observation would draw on tactile information at the gripper–furniture interface. The question is which differences, if any, carry enough information to separate slip at that interface from drift in the map-frame localization estimate. It does not name a particular prediction model.
Would a large tactile shear reading by itself answer the question?

No. Tactile shear is relevant to the contact, but a shear reading alone is not a stated test for relative slip, much less a test that excludes map-frame localization drift. The proposed comparison is tactile–odometric: it asks whether the contact information is consistent with the motion information. Even then, a proposed residual pattern would need justification before being treated as a reliable discriminator.
Why specify gripper–furniture slip instead of simply saying ‘object slip’?

It locates the possible relative motion at the gripper–furniture interface. That matters for interpreting a contact residual: the question is whether the furniture is slipping relative to the gripper, as distinct from the estimated pose drifting in the map frame. It does not define another slip location or a broader set of failure categories.
And what does ‘map-frame’ add to localization drift?

It identifies the reference frame in which the localization estimate might drift. Gripper–furniture slip is about a relative relationship at contact; map-frame localization drift is about the estimated placement in the map. A tactile–odometric comparison can be informative about relative contact consistency without necessarily providing an independent check of absolute map-frame placement. Keeping those two reference relationships separate is central to the question.
Suppose tactile and odometric information agree during an occlusion. Does that prove there was no localization drift?

No. Agreement can mean that the available relative information is mutually consistent, but it need not establish that the map-frame pose estimate is correct. If a map-frame error leaves the locally compared quantities unchanged, that comparison alone cannot reveal it. Agreement should therefore not be promoted to proof that localization has not drifted.
Does a disagreement prove gripper–furniture slip, then?

Not automatically. A disagreement is a candidate indication that the assumed contact relationship and the available observations do not fit together. The question is whether a particular tactile–odometric residual can attribute that disagreement to gripper–furniture slip rather than map-frame localization drift. No threshold, attribution rule, or demonstrated result is supplied.
How do the five-second RGB-D occlusions affect what can be claimed?

During each five-second RGB-D occlusion, the comparison cannot assume a fresh RGB-D observation. It must be framed around what tactile and odometric information can say over that interval. The specified duration matters: this asks about discrimination during five-second gaps, not about continuously available RGB-D or an unspecified period without vision. The wording does not say how many such gaps occur or provide observations from them.
Could RGB-D after an occlusion settle what happened inside those five seconds?

An observation when RGB-D becomes available again could provide additional information, but the question specifically asks which tactile–odometric residuals distinguish the two explanations during five-second RGB-D occlusions. It does not state that a later observation uniquely reconstructs what happened within a gap. Treating later RGB-D as a guaranteed answer would go beyond the question.
Is there a useful way to describe a candidate residual without inventing its mathematical form?

Yes: describe it as the discrepancy between tactile evidence about the gripper–furniture contact and contact behavior expected from wheel-odometric motion. That conveys what would be compared while leaving open how tactile shear is represented, how motion is projected to the contact, and how the discrepancy is evaluated. Those choices are not specified in the question.
Could I say that a contact-consistency residual distinguishes slip, while a map-position residual distinguishes drift?

That would be too definite as written. Contact consistency is a plausible place to look for evidence of gripper–furniture slip. But a map-position residual requires some basis for comparing estimated map-frame position with something independent; the question does not supply a map-frame observation during the five-second RGB-D occlusions. More importantly, it asks *which* residuals distinguish the explanations—it does not assert that either proposed residual already does so.
So is the difficult part the difference between detecting inconsistency and identifying its source?

Exactly. A residual can indicate that a contact or motion prediction does not match an observation. The stronger claim is that its behavior separates relative slip at the gripper–furniture interface from drift in map-frame localization. The question asks for that stronger separation under five-second RGB-D occlusions, rather than merely for any signal that something is inconsistent.
Would it help to compare residuals over the whole five-second interval rather than one instant?

Considering their behavior across the occlusion is a reasonable way to frame the inquiry, but the question does not specify whether the discriminator uses an instantaneous value, a time history, or both. Whichever description is used, it remains a question about whether tactile–odometric information over a five-second RGB-D gap can distinguish gripper–furniture slip from map-frame localization drift.
Is it possible that tactile and wheel-odometric information alone cannot resolve map-frame drift during the gap?

That is an important possibility to leave open. If the available comparison only constrains motion and contact relative to the manipulator, a change in the estimated map-frame placement may not have a distinct signature in it. Whether the proposed estimator has another relevant constraint is not specified here. The question should not be answered with a guarantee of discrimination that the supplied information does not support.
Then how can I phrase the research question precisely without implying an answer?

‘Which residuals between tactile contact information and wheel odometry, if any, distinguish gripper–furniture slip from map-frame localization drift during five-second RGB-D occlusions?’ Adding ‘if any’ makes the uncertainty explicit. It preserves the two specific explanations, the tactile–odometric comparison, and the five-second visual gap without presupposing a successful residual or a measured result.
Should the explanation also keep the furniture-control context, or would that change the question?

You can mention furniture control as the context for why the distinction matters. The question itself remains about identifying informative tactile–odometric residuals during five-second RGB-D occlusions. Mentioning the context does not establish that a particular residual has been selected, that a controller responds in a specified way, or that any performance target has been achieved.
Can we state a hypothesis about which signals distinguish the two explanations during the five-second RGB-D occlusions?

The hypothesis is that, during five-second RGB-D occlusions, shear transients indicate slip, while shear-stable wheel–contact residuals indicate drift. It predicts that using this distinction will yield at least 90% balanced accuracy for identifying slip versus drift. Those are proposed signal interpretations and a predicted performance level, not established findings.
What is a shear transient supposed to mean in that statement?

It means a change in the tactile shear signal, as opposed to shear that remains stable over the relevant period. The hypothesis treats such transients as indicators of slip at the gripper–furniture contact. It does not specify a numerical size, duration, or threshold for a transient, and it does not claim that every change in shear conclusively proves slip.
Is ‘shear-stable’ just another way of saying there is no slip?

No. The drift side of the hypothesis is specifically about shear-stable *wheel–contact residuals*. Stable shear is part of the proposed pattern, not a stand-alone proof that slip is absent or that map-frame localization has drifted. The interpretation depends on the residual in conjunction with that shear condition.
What does the wheel–contact residual represent at this level of detail?

It is a way of expressing a discrepancy between motion indicated by the wheels and behavior expected at the furniture contact. The hypothesis names wheel–contact residuals but does not define their equation, reference frame, sign, or decision threshold. It proposes that their behavior when shear is stable indicates localization drift rather than gripper–furniture slip.
Why does the hypothesis use different kinds of evidence for the two cases?

It proposes two contrasting signatures: a transient in tactile shear for slip, and a wheel–contact residual under stable shear for drift. Conceptually, the first points to a change at the contact, while the second points to an inconsistency that persists in the motion–contact comparison without a corresponding shear transient. That is the proposed interpretation; whether those signatures actually separate the cases well enough remains to be determined.
Does it claim that shear transients and shear-stable residuals can never occur together?

No. It does not specify a rule for overlapping, ambiguous, or absent signatures. The stated hypothesis identifies patterns expected to indicate each explanation and predicts classification performance; it does not assert that every possible observation fits neatly into exactly one pattern.
The earlier question was about gripper–furniture slip versus map-frame localization drift. Should I keep that specificity when explaining the hypothesis?

Yes. In this context, ‘slip’ refers to gripper–furniture slip and ‘drift’ to map-frame localization drift. Keeping those meanings clear helps avoid treating a contact-relative change and a map-frame estimation error as interchangeable. The hypothesis associates shear transients with the former and shear-stable wheel–contact residuals with the latter.
Could I write that wheel odometry detects localization drift directly?

That would be stronger than the hypothesis. It proposes that *shear-stable wheel–contact residuals* indicate drift. It does not say wheel odometry alone directly observes map-frame error or provides an independent ground-truth map position.
And could I say tactile shear alone identifies all slip events?

No. The proposed slip indicator is shear transients during the specified occlusions. The hypothesis does not say that all slip events necessarily produce a detectable transient, or that tactile shear alone resolves every case. Its quantitative claim is a prediction of at least 90% balanced accuracy, not perfect identification.
Why is the five-second RGB-D occlusion condition essential rather than incidental?

It sets the condition under which these signatures are hypothesized to work. During a five-second RGB-D occlusion, the distinction cannot depend on a fresh RGB-D observation within that gap. Restating the hypothesis without that condition would make it sound broader than stated; changing the duration would also alter the claim.
Is the prediction about performance only after RGB-D becomes available again?

No. The hypothesis is phrased around identifying slip versus drift *during five-second RGB-D occlusions* using the stated shear and wheel–contact patterns. It does not specify a later RGB-D-based reconstruction or say that classification must wait for visibility to return.
What exactly does ‘yielding ≥90% balanced accuracy’ commit the hypothesis to?

It predicts at least 90% balanced accuracy in distinguishing slip from drift under the stated condition. For the two categories, balanced accuracy weights correct recognition of each category equally. The ≥ sign matters: the predicted level is 90% or higher, not exactly 90%. It remains a hypothesis rather than a reported measurement.
Does that mean at least 90% correct separately for slip and for drift?

Not necessarily. Balanced accuracy is the average of the recognition rates for the two categories. A balanced accuracy of at least 90% does not, by itself, state that each category individually reaches at least 90%. The hypothesis supplies the combined balanced-accuracy target, not separate per-category targets.
Should I connect that 90% prediction to the furniture repositioning distance target?

Only by distinguishing their roles. This hypothesis predicts at least 90% balanced accuracy for slip-versus-drift identification during five-second RGB-D occlusions. It does not predict a repositioning distance or state that distinguishing the two explanations, by itself, achieves the furniture-repositioning requirement.
If I say ‘a stable shear signal proves the map frame has drifted,’ what is missing?

The wheel–contact residual is missing, and ‘proves’ overstates the claim. The proposed drift indicator is a shear-stable wheel–contact residual. Even with that full pattern, ‘indicates drift’ is the hypothesis’s wording; it is not a statement of certainty or an observed validation result.
How could the hypothesis be written compactly without obscuring that it is untested?

‘We hypothesize that, during five-second RGB-D occlusions, shear transients indicate gripper–furniture slip, whereas shear-stable wheel–contact residuals indicate map-frame localization drift, yielding ≥90% balanced accuracy in distinguishing the two.’ This retains the duration, both proposed signatures, the two explanations, and the predicted metric while explicitly marking the claim as a hypothesis.
Would ‘whereas’ imply these are exhaustive and infallible rules?

Not when they are clearly introduced as a hypothesis about indicators. ‘Whereas’ contrasts the proposed signatures; it does not supply an exhaustive decision procedure or guarantee an unambiguous result in every instance. The predicted ≥90% balanced accuracy is itself different from claiming infallibility.
What should remain open at this point?

Whether the proposed shear-transient and shear-stable wheel–contact patterns actually distinguish gripper–furniture slip from map-frame localization drift during five-second RGB-D occlusions remains open. The hypothesis also leaves the residual definition and any handling of ambiguous signals unspecified. None of those details should be presented as a completed test or settled result.
What is the plan for examining slip versus drift during the RGB-D occlusions?

The plan has three parts: label slip and drift using motion capture only for training, train a shear–odometry classifier on those labels, and evaluate it on unseen furniture through five-second RGB-D occlusions without external tracking. That is a proposed sequence of work, not a report that training or evaluation has happened.
What does ‘training-only motion capture’ limit?

It limits motion capture to the labeling used for training. The evaluation on unseen furniture is to take place without external tracking. A description of the plan should not quietly make motion capture available to the classifier or the manipulator during that evaluation.
Are the motion-capture labels the classifier’s inputs?

They are the intended training labels: they identify slip or drift for examples used to train the classifier. The classifier is described as a shear–odometry classifier, so its stated inputs are shear and odometry, not motion capture. The plan does not specify the exact form of those inputs or the labeling procedure.
Could I describe motion capture as a third sensor in the classifier?

No. That would change its role. Motion capture is proposed for training-only labeling; the classifier to be trained is based on shear and odometry. Keeping those roles separate is especially important because the planned evaluation is without external tracking.
Does the plan say how motion capture will determine whether a training example is slip or drift?

No. It says to label slip and drift with training-only motion capture, but it does not give a labeling rule, a threshold, or a procedure for resolving ambiguous examples. Those details remain unspecified rather than being implicit results of the plan.
What exactly would the classifier be trained to distinguish?

It would be trained to distinguish slip from drift using shear and odometry. In the furniture-contact context, those terms refer to gripper–furniture slip and map-frame localization drift. The plan does not specify a classifier architecture, a particular residual equation, or additional output categories.
Should I say that the classifier explicitly computes the wheel–contact residual we discussed?

Not as a settled design detail. The plan specifies a shear–odometry classifier but does not say whether it computes a named wheel–contact residual, uses another representation of those signals, or combines several features. You can describe residuals as the question motivating the work without attributing an unprovided calculation to the classifier.
Why mention the five-second occlusions in the evaluation step?

They define the visual-gap condition through which the unseen-furniture evaluation is planned. The duration is five seconds, and the occlusions are of RGB-D. The plan should not be recast as evaluation with continuous RGB-D visibility or with gaps of an unspecified length.
Does five seconds also specify how long each training example is?

No. The five-second duration describes the RGB-D occlusions in the planned evaluation. The plan does not specify a training-example length, a classifier input window, or how frequently the classifier produces a decision.
Would it be accurate to say RGB-D is an input to this classifier?

The classifier in this plan is specified as shear–odometry, so RGB-D should not be added as a stated classifier input. RGB-D appears in the evaluation condition: the unseen-furniture evaluation runs through five-second RGB-D occlusions. The plan does not spell out what role RGB-D plays outside those occlusions.
When you say ‘unseen furniture,’ what can we safely claim about the evaluation items?

The evaluation is planned on unseen furniture. The plan does not define the precise criterion for ‘unseen,’ identify furniture types, or give a partitioning procedure. Those details should not be supplied as though they were already specified.
Is evaluation on unseen furniture the same as claiming the classifier will generalize successfully?
No. Unseen furniture is the planned evaluation condition, not an observed outcome. Whether the classifier distinguishes slip from drift successfully under that condition remains to be evaluated.
I am concerned that ‘without external tracking’ might be misunderstood as ‘without any observations.’

It does not mean that. The stated classifier is based on shear and odometry; ‘without external tracking’ restricts the planned evaluation’s reliance on external tracking. It does not say that all sensing is absent. At the same time, it does not specify every observation or resource available during evaluation.
Can motion capture be used to check decisions during the unseen-furniture evaluation, since it would not be fed to the classifier?

The plan says motion capture is for training-only labeling and calls for evaluation without external tracking. It would be inaccurate to present motion capture as part of that evaluation merely because it is not fed directly into the classifier. The plan does not specify how evaluation labels or scores will be obtained without introducing external tracking.
Does that leave an open question about measuring evaluation performance?

Yes. The plan states where training labels come from and the condition under which evaluation is to occur, but it does not describe a separate evaluation-labeling or scoring procedure. That omission should be left open rather than filled with an invented measurement method.
Is the planned evaluation specifically a test of furniture repositioning accuracy?

The plan says to evaluate on unseen furniture through five-second occlusions without external tracking. It does not specify an evaluation metric or say exactly how repositioning accuracy and slip-versus-drift identification would be scored. Furniture repositioning is the surrounding task context, but a particular measurement procedure is not part of this plan.
Does the plan promise a particular balanced accuracy for the classifier?

No measured or guaranteed accuracy is stated in the plan. It calls for training and evaluation; it does not report classifier performance or specify an achieved result. Any outcome would have to remain open at this stage.
Would it be fair to say the sequence is label, train, then evaluate?

Yes. First, use training-only motion capture to label slip and drift; then train a shear–odometry classifier; then evaluate on unseen furniture through five-second RGB-D occlusions without external tracking. That sequence captures the plan without adding a model design, dataset size, or result.
Does the plan require retraining the classifier during evaluation?

It does not state any retraining during evaluation. The described sequence separates training with motion-capture-derived labels from evaluation without external tracking. A specific online adaptation or retraining procedure would be an additional design choice, not something established here.
Could I phrase the plan in one compact sentence?

‘Use motion capture only to label slip and drift for training, train a shear–odometry classifier, and evaluate it on unseen furniture through five-second RGB-D occlusions without external tracking.’ That preserves the separate roles of motion capture and the classifier, as well as the furniture and occlusion conditions of the planned evaluation.
And if someone asks whether this already shows that shear and odometry distinguish the two cases?

The answer is no: this is a plan to train and evaluate a classifier for that distinction. It does not contain evaluation outcomes. Its value as a description is that it makes the proposed training-label source, classifier inputs, and evaluation conditions explicit without treating the intended result as already observed.
What activity would evaluate the proposed slip-versus-drift distinction?

Run 120 OccludedFurniture trials on unseen furniture with induced slip or localization drift. Ablate shear and score balanced accuracy during the five-second occlusions. That specifies an evaluation activity; it does not report that the trials have been run or that any accuracy has been achieved.
Should ‘OccludedFurniture’ stay in the description?
Yes. OccludedFurniture is the specific trial name in the activity, so it is worth preserving. The activity calls for 120 OccludedFurniture trials, not merely an unspecified set of furniture trials.
What does the number 120 count?

It counts trials: the activity is to run 120 OccludedFurniture trials. It does not say there are 120 examples of slip and another 120 of drift, or specify how the trials are divided between those conditions.
Does ‘unseen furniture’ describe the objects used for those trials?
Yes. The 120 trials are to be run on unseen furniture. The activity does not name the furniture, define exactly what makes it unseen, or state how many distinct pieces are involved.
Why induce slip or localization drift rather than just wait for a discrepancy to occur?

The stated activity uses induced slip or localization drift so that the trials include the two conditions whose distinction is at issue. It does not specify how either condition is induced or claim that an induced condition perfectly reproduces every naturally occurring instance.
Does ‘slip or localization drift’ mean both must be induced simultaneously in each trial?

No. The wording names slip or localization drift as the induced conditions; it does not say to induce both simultaneously in every trial. It also does not specify a per-trial schedule, class counts, or whether any additional conditions are included.
Can we keep the earlier distinction between the two conditions clear?

Does the activity require scoring how often the same move has both a correct identification and a placement within 5 cm?
No combined measure is specified. It calls for slip/drift accuracy and post-run 5-cm success, but does not prescribe a joint success rate or a push-by-push analysis linking the two.
Is contact loss a third scored outcome here?

No. Maintaining contact is part of the broader furniture-manipulation goal, but this activity specifically names identification accuracy and post-run 5-cm success as measurements. It gives neither a contact-loss scoring procedure nor a contact-preservation result.
Does ‘micro-dither’ mean the manipulator breaks contact to probe the furniture?

No such release is specified. The selected policy involves contact micro-dithers, but the activity does not detail their physical execution or report whether contact remained unbroken during all 100 moves. A diagnostic contact action should not be paraphrased as an instruction to release the furniture.
Does the activity say what control action follows a slip or drift classification?

No. It says to execute the moves using the selected policy and measure two outcomes, but does not define the controller’s response to either label or a placement-correction sequence. Those would be additional task-specific procedures.
Could I say the five-second gaps are used to obtain the post-run placement measurement?

No. The five-second occlusions are a condition of execution. The placement measurement is post-run. The activity does not specify the measurement instrument or say the final error is measured during an occlusion.
Is an execution-time external tracker stated as part of this test?

No tracking equipment is specified in this activity. The broader goal requires identification without external tracking during execution, but the wording here gives no additional tracking or scoring setup. It would be inappropriate to insert an external tracker into the activity as though it were prescribed.
Can we treat this as a completed validation of both performance requirements?

No. It is an execution and measurement activity. It supplies no slip/drift accuracy, no number of post-run placements within 5 cm, and no separate contact-maintenance finding. Results would have to be reported before either performance outcome could be assessed.
How would you state the activity in one sentence while keeping the two measurements distinct?

‘Execute 100 unseen-furniture moves using the selected gating/micro-dither policy through five-second RGB-D occlusions, measuring slip-versus-drift accuracy and post-run within-5-cm placement success.’
What details should remain open after stating it that way?

The achieved identification accuracy, post-run success count, number of occlusions and micro-dither triggers, labeling and placement-measurement procedures, and contact-maintenance outcome all remain unstated. The activity fixes the 100-move count, unseen-furniture condition, selected policy, five-second occlusions, and two measures to collect.
What does the GatedDither-100 report contain?

The GatedDither-100 report contains per-trial slip/drift predictions, post-run placement errors, occlusion intervals, and contact-loss flags for 100 moves. That identifies four kinds of records; it does not provide their values or an aggregate performance result.
Does the name mean there are 100 predictions?

No. The stated count is 100 moves. The report contains predictions on a per-trial basis, but it does not specify exactly how many predictions were made within each move or the total number of classification decisions.
What do the slip/drift predictions represent?

They record which of the two explanations was predicted: slip at the furniture contact or localization drift. They are predictions, not necessarily verified labels. The artifact description does not say what any individual prediction was or whether it was correct.
Are reference slip and drift labels also listed?

They are not among the stated contents. The report is described as containing slip/drift predictions, but no reference-label field or confusion matrix is specified. Predictions alone cannot establish balanced accuracy without an appropriate reference and scoring rule.
Could I calculate slip/drift balanced accuracy just by knowing there were 100 moves?

No. Balanced accuracy requires the correct-recognition rates for slip and drift. The move count does not provide reference labels, class counts, or the number of scored decisions per move. Nor does the report description give a balanced-accuracy value.
How are the post-run placement errors different from the predictions?

The predictions concern identifying slip versus drift; the post-run placement errors concern where the furniture ended up after a move. A correct identification would not, by itself, specify the final placement error, and a post-run error would not reveal whether the slip/drift prediction was correct.
Does ‘post-run’ tell us anything about positioning during the move?

It limits what is stated: the named placement errors are assessed after the runs. Their presence does not establish a continuous record of furniture-position error during each move or within an occlusion interval.
Does the report give a within-5-cm success rate?

No success rate is among the contents explicitly named. It contains post-run placement errors, which are relevant to assessing a 5-cm placement criterion, but no error values, success count, or aggregate rate are provided in the artifact description.
If I had the individual errors, could I simply count those within 5 cm?

Those post-run errors would be relevant to counting placements that meet a 5-cm tolerance. The description here, though, does not show the errors or define the detailed scoring procedure, so it does not itself tell us how many of the 100 moves qualified.
What are the occlusion intervals in the report?

They are the recorded intervals during which occlusion occurred for the moves. The description does not show their individual timing, say how many intervals occurred per move, or state what the other report fields did at particular points within them.
Does the report’s list say that there was exactly one occlusion interval in each move?
No. It names occlusion intervals among the report contents without giving a per-move count. The 100 refers to moves, not to intervals.
Can I infer from an occlusion interval that a slip prediction was made during it?

Not from the list of contents alone. The report includes predictions and occlusion intervals, but the description does not specify decision timestamps or link any particular prediction to any particular interval. Such a relationship would have to be established from the records themselves.
What does a contact-loss flag record?

It is a per-trial indicator relating to whether contact was lost. Having contact-loss flags in the report is not the same as reporting how many were set, whether any were set, or how long any loss lasted. The description does not give a contact-loss count.
Would a flag showing no contact loss prove there was no slip?

No. Slip can involve relative movement while contact remains established. Contact loss and slip/drift identification are distinct questions; the report lists flags and predictions separately and does not specify what any individual record shows.
Do the contact-loss flags tell us the size of the force used for a micro-dither?
No. A contact-loss flag is not a force measurement. The stated report contents do not include force values, micro-dither trajectories, or a numerical force limit.
Can I say the report shows which moves triggered micro-dithers?

That is not among the specified fields. The report’s name identifies the artifact, but its stated contents are predictions, post-run placement errors, occlusion intervals, and contact-loss flags. It does not expressly list trigger events or ceiling-inlier recovery times.
Does the name tell us how the ceiling gate behaved in each move?
No. ‘GatedDither-100’ names the report. It does not, by itself, supply gate durations, feature-inlier records, branch selections, or a record of when micro-dithers occurred.
Could the report establish how often correct predictions and within-5-cm placement happened together?

The described records could be relevant to examining identification and placement on a per-trial basis, but the description does not include reference slip/drift labels or the placement-error values. It does not state a joint success rate or define how multiple predictions within one move would be matched to its post-run error.
Do the occlusion intervals and contact-loss flags establish whether contact was maintained throughout every occlusion?

Not from the artifact description. It lists both types of record, but supplies no flag values or their temporal resolution. We cannot conclude whether contact was lost during an interval, outside it, or not at all.
Is there an external-tracking record in the listed contents?

No external-tracking record is specified. The report description also does not explain how post-run errors or reference classifications were obtained. It would be inappropriate to insert a measurement instrument based only on this list.
Does having records for 100 moves mean every field is complete for every move?

The report is described as containing those categories of records for 100 moves, but it does not give a completeness audit or state that every possible field was populated and valid in every trial. That cannot be assumed as a separate finding.
How should I describe what a reader can inspect without claiming results?

A reader can look to the GatedDither-100 report for the per-trial slip/drift predictions, post-run placement errors, occlusion intervals, and contact-loss flags associated with the 100 moves. That describes the available kinds of records without saying what the predictions were, how large the errors were, or whether any contact was lost.
Could I call it a report of achieved 5-cm placement and no contact loss?
No. It contains placement errors and contact-loss flags, but their values are not supplied here. The presence of a field for an outcome does not establish a favorable result for that outcome.
Give me a one-sentence description that keeps all four contents and the count.
‘The GatedDither-100 report contains per-trial slip/drift predictions, post-run placement errors, occlusion intervals, and contact-loss flags for 100 furniture moves.’
What is the most important distinction when someone reads that sentence?
It describes what the report records, not what its records show. No balanced accuracy, within-5-cm success count, occlusion-interval count, or contact-loss rate is stated in the artifact description.
